title: Linear A and Linear B Side by Side
short: The same sign shapes, different languages: what we know about each script, what we don't, and why Linear B could be read when Linear A cannot.
trouble: Students think Linear A and Linear B are two languages written the same way, or the same language. They share signs, but Linear B writes Greek and Linear A an unknown language.

blocks.html: This last lesson puts the two scripts of the course side by side. You have learned Linear B from its signs to its tablets, and Linear A from its corpus to How to Judge a Decipherment Claim. Here is what they share, what divides them and why one can be read.

Linear A and Linear B share many sign shapes and the same numbers, but they write different languages: Linear B writes Greek, Linear A an unknown language. Linear B could be read because it had a known language, a large corpus and good tests; Linear A has none of these yet.

blocks.html: Why do the shared signs not make Linear A readable? Shapes can be borrowed while languages differ. The Latin alphabet writes English, French and Turkish; knowing the letters lets you sound out a Turkish sentence but not understand it. Linear A is in the same position, except that its sounds are themselves only a convention.

Thinking Linear A and Linear B are two languages written the same way, or the same language. They share signs, but Linear B writes Greek and Linear A an unknown language. Check: if a text is in Linear B, you can read it as Greek; if it is in Linear A, you can sound it out by convention but not read it.
